messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina is a forty-two-year-old woman who came to the United States from a West African country eight years ago, after surviving a period of detention and torture by members of a local militia. She had been a community organizer, and when the militia took control of her town, they arrested her along with several others. For three weeks she was held in a concrete room that smelled sharply of mildew, sweat, and old blood. Her captors interrogated her daily, sometimes with fists, sometimes with a rubber hose, sometimes with a plastic bag over her head until she lost consciousness. She remembers the damp chill of that room, the way rain leaked through a crack in the ceiling and fell onto her shoulder. She remembers a guard named Paul who would call her by name each time he entered, his voice flat, almost bored. She still cannot hear the name Paul without her chest tightening. The weather that entire period was gray and cold, with a constant drizzle. Now, whenever the sky turns that same shade of pewter and a light rain begins, she feels the old dread settle into her bones before her mind has caught up to what is happening.

In the factory where she works on an assembly line, physical proximity is unavoidable. Coworkers stand inches from her, sometimes brushing against her arm. When someone steps too close from behind, she flinches so hard that she has dropped parts more than once. Her supervisor has warned her about her "nerves." She has learned to keep her face still, but inside she is already scanning the room for exits. At home, she listens intently for any sound that might mean someone is entering—the creak of a floorboard, the click of a lock. She jumps at ordinary noises: a car horn, a door slamming, a pan dropping in the kitchen. Her body reacts before her conscious mind can intervene, flooding her with adrenaline for no reason she can name in the moment.

The memory of the detention room sometimes comes to her in fragments that feel disconnected from her own life. When she thinks about it, she can smell the mildew and the metallic tang of blood, and she thinks, *This cannot have happened to me*. It feels like a story she once heard, or a film she watched, not something that belongs to her. Sometimes the memory feels as though it belongs to someone else entirely, and she watches it from a distance. But then her body betrays her: a sudden sweat, a racing heart, the urge to run. She has come to believe that her body is no longer trustworthy. It sends alarms that have no clear cause and fails to protect her when real danger is past. She no longer feels capable of doing the things that used to define her—speaking in public, standing up for others, even holding a simple conversation without her mind fleeing to the past. The world, she is certain, is a dangerous place, and she is not equipped to navigate it.

To cope, Amina has developed a set of strategies that keep her functioning, though barely. She wears heavy makeup every day—foundation, concealer, powder—not to look pretty, but to feel as though she is wearing a mask, as if the person looking back from the mirror is someone else, someone who was never in that room. She avoids wearing any clothes that resemble the ones she wore during her detention: a dark blue blouse and black pants. She has thrown away every item of that color and now dresses only in bright patterns or white, desperate to distance herself from that version of herself. Her mind is never idle. At work, she counts parts, sings songs in her head, recites the steps of her tasks over and over—anything to keep from slipping into a memory. At night, she turns on the television and forces herself to follow the plot, even when she is exhausted.

These strategies have come at a cost. Her marriage ended three years ago, in part because her husband could not understand why she would not let him touch her from behind, why she sometimes woke screaming, why she would not talk about where she had been. She has lost touch with the few friends she made in her first years here. She does not go out unless she must. At work, she keeps to herself. The isolation is heavy, but the alternative—letting her guard down—feels impossible.

She came to therapy after a string of bad weeks. The weather turned cold and rainy. A new worker started on her line whose name is Paul. She heard someone call him that, and she had to excuse herself to the bathroom, where she stood trembling and crying, unable to stop smelling the mildew and old blood. That evening, she checked every lock four times, then sat on the floor in the corner of her bedroom until dawn. She realized she could not keep living this way. What she hopes for, though she hardly dares to name it, is to stop being afraid of her own skin. What she fears most is that the person she used to be is gone forever, and that the only thing left is this body that does not feel like hers, living in a world that will never feel safe.
